title: Award-Winning Photographer Kent Porter Captures Night Skies in All Their Glory
summary:
From sunset to sunrise, the night sky becomes a canvas for stories written in — and among — the stars.

The post Award-Winning Photographer Kent Porter Captures Night Skies in All Their Glory appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
From our earliest years, stories, poems, and lullabies guide our eyes heavenward to wonder and wish upon stars and find comfort in the gentle glow of the moon ushering us into slumber. For photographer Kent Porter, the hushed twinkle of the night skies are a creative and quiet respite from the rigors of covering the news for The Press Democrat.

“When I get really stressed out — even during disasters — I’ll wait around till everyone’s gone home and shoot night pictures,” says Porter.

There are times at twilight when the lunar ascent is so arresting we feel compelled to pull a phone from our pockets and snap some shots, which often confirm that taking a great photo of the heavens is more skill than happenstance. While Porter freely admits there is some luck involved in his evening endeavors, his most captivating images have been earned through years of practice and patience and learned in the self-guided study of astronomy, which provides certain epiphanies.

“The moon is daylight,” he says. “It’s just reflecting the sun. It’s a different shade of daylight.”

Though he receives invitations to set up on private land to capture his images of streaking comets and rippling auroras, Porter prefers to make his photos in public spaces. It’s proof, he says, of what’s available to all of us “with a little bit of effort and a little bit of driving.” The drives take him far from city lights, tramping across fields, scrambling up hills, and leaping over ditches until he finds exactly the right spot where he can feel the firmament’s magic.

“It’s like the stars are sitting on you,” he says. “They look like they’re dropping right on you. Trying to re-create that in a photo is my main goal.”

Knights Valley, October 2019

During the second week of the Kincade Fire, flames swept through Knights Valley, igniting a lone Valley Oak that threw off embers in the breeze. Having passed by it once and noticing how many photographers were making images of the tree, I decided I wasn’t going to make the same photograph. When I passed by it again, only one photographer remained. About a mile down the road, I made a 180. I decided to take a different approach by changing the angle to include Mount St. Helena. I made 10 different frames of the scene, the tenth being the best when the meteorite flashed during the long exposure. Lucky.

Canon R5 camera, 35 mm lens, F4.5 at ISO 800, 12-second exposure

Healdsburg, November 2025

Those who can’t afford a trip to view the Northern Lights keep a close watch on Coronal Mass Ejections, or CMEs, bursts of plasma hurled toward Earth from the sun. The last several years, the sun has been in a solar maximum, raising the possibility Northern Lights could be viewable in the lower 48 states. Tracking the space weather forecast last November, I headed out soon after sunset. As night fell, cloudy skies obstructed the horizon, but I realized the cloud cover wouldn’t dampen the colors. Sensing a near-historic display, I headed from my perch in The Geysers to Dry Creek Road, ending up at Timber Crest Farms with artificial light illuminating the scene. Watching the pillars shimmer across the night sky, I got goosebumps witnessing something so alien and beautiful take shape in the viewfinder.

Canon R5 camera, 35 mm lens, F4.0 at ISO 800, 13-second exposure

Bodega Bay, September 2025

During the fall months, Porter heads to the coast on dark, moonless nights to check out seasonal bioluminescence. As waves crash ashore, the surf turns electric blue, stirring millions of dinoflagellates when a chemical reaction takes place.

“The Milky Way was a plus, and even more unanticipated was the person on the beach with a headlamp, giving the photograph a layered view of the surroundings,” says Porter.

Canon R5 camera, 31 mm lens, F4.0 at ISO 5,000, 15-second exposure

Santa Rosa, July 2025

“Fireworks used to give me fits,” Porter says of film cameras. With those he ended up with more unusable photos than good ones. Digital cameras allow photographers to adjust shutter speeds and F-stops as they go.

“My advice is this: Arrive early, stake out a spot, and stick with it. Then, after realizing the spot you picked out really bites for foreground and maximum burst potential, move in a hurry, trip over several people in the dark, block a few others, and finally pick an area which looks OK through a dark camera and be surprised the first spot was probably much better after all,” says Porter with his dry sense of humor.

Another pro-tip? “The finale never looks good through a camera. Photojournalists don’t stack images, so the final frenzy is almost always too bright with too much smoke.”

Canon R5 camera, 23 mm lens, F10.0 at ISO 100, 30-second exposure

Glen Ellen, December 2024

The Super Cold Moon in December 2024 called for a different location than the other full moon locations Porter uses.

“I had a good understanding of what I wanted in the foreground after a hike I made several years prior at Sonoma Valley Regional Park,” says Porter, who noticed how stark the landscape was with the denuded vegetation on the trees left after the Nuns Fire.

“We don’t have many identifiable landmarks in Sonoma County, such as the Golden Gate or Bay bridges or the Transamerica building. Finding a foreground where the moon is at its largest can be daunting, so I settle for mountains and trees.”

Canon R5, 560 mm lens, F4.0 at ISO 800, 1/320th of a second exposure

The Geysers, August 2020

A dry lightning outbreak hammered Northern California resulting in fires that burned more than 2.5 million acres within a 75-mile radius of Sonoma County. The weather forecast hinted at a lightning bust (a weather phenomenon referring to an electric storm that ignites a large number of wildfires simultaneously), but even seasoned weather forecasters were surprised by the ferocity of the storm.

Being in position early was critical to making a storytelling image. Along with lightning, there were several heat bursts associated with the early morning outbreak. At my position in The Geysers, the temperature spiked at 96 degrees, making the surreal scene more impressive. All five strikes in the image occurred at the same time.

Canon 5D Mark IV camera, 70 mm lens, F4.5 at ISO 100, 20-second exposure

Near The Geysers, October 2024

I did a test shoot of comet C/2023 A3 Tsuchinshan-ATLAS of this scene and failed miserably. I was up too far, wrong lens, wrong exposure, and too late to get any glow of the sunset.

So, I arrived early the next evening, hiked down a steep ravine with two cameras, lenses, and a tripod. I wanted the oak tree in the frame, so it might give a sense of place, and descended deeper down the mountainside. I lined everything up perfectly for a deep vertical image. The only thing I forgot was a headlamp to navigate back up the hill, twisting my ankles in deep cow hoof indentations in the dry, crusty soil. This photograph remains one of my favorite images due to the planning involved.

Canon R5 camera, 100 mm lens, F5.0 at ISO 400, eight-second exposure

Healdsburg, April 2026

I’m always looking to the sky and the clouds to gauge the quality of a sunset. During transition months, when stormy weather and high pressure systems meet, the result is spectacular sunsets, like the one at this varsity baseball game between Analy and Healdsburg high schools. Having a few seconds between innings to get a sunset image with a foreground, the umpire stood in the right place to give me a semblance of composition.

Canon R5 camera, 15 mm lens, F3.2, at ISO 100, 1/100th-second exposure

The post Award-Winning Photographer Kent Porter Captures Night Skies in All Their Glory appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: The Camino de Sonoma Offers Hikers a Physical and Spiritual Journey
summary:
The Camino de Sonoma — an epic, six-stage pilgrimage from Sonoma to Fort Ross — becomes a transformational odyssey for intrepid hikers.

The post The Camino de Sonoma Offers Hikers a Physical and Spiritual Journey appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Steven Winter, known to some as Steven the Elder, is the first to mention Billy Goat Hill.

“I thought I was gonna die,” he tells me less than five minutes after I park my car, ready to embark upon my first-ever Camino de Sonoma, a six-stage, 85-mile spiritual walk from the mission in Sonoma to Fort Ross on the coast. “I think there was one part I prayed to die, like take me now,” Winter, a trail volunteer and retired Sonoma State kinesiology professor, remembers thinking during his first Camino de Sonoma experience. “I’ve lived a good 60 years. I do not want to finish this hill.”

I’d heard stories about pilgrims suffering along the ancient Camino de Santiago in Europe, but what exactly was I getting into?

“We don’t do interviews, we do walks,” Camino de Sonoma co-founder Adam Peacocke told me from the beginning. A pastor who followed in his father’s footsteps, both in the pulpit and on the football field, he has a very pragmatic way of building the trail narrative one “intentional step” at a time.

So I committed to walking Stage 1 from Sonoma to Kenwood, and planned to catch up with the group five days later at Stage 6 for the final 13.5-mile climb from Jenner to Fort Ross, which included the infamous Billy Goat Hill.

Soon after meeting Steven the Elder and co-founder Tony “Camino” McCormick, who has completed the circuit so many times (41 and counting) he took on the name of the trail, we gather in a circle in Sonoma Plaza and introduce ourselves. Dino Franklin Jr., a former tribal chairman for the Kashia Band of Pomo Indians and Camino board member, quickly sets the tone. “It’s hard for me to be in this area right here,” he says, admonishing the group of more than 20 bright-eyed, eager hikers.

The bronze Bear Flag Monument towers behind us, and just across the street lies Mission San Francisco Solano. “I know for you guys, you get to see how beautiful this town is. But for me, I’m reminded about what’s in the ground, the blood, the babies, all that was shed for that little place right here to be built,” Franklin says, gesturing toward the whitewashed adobe chapel.

That painfully honest history is something that will come up again and again, in murals, markers, and trailside stories over the next week. Peacocke often describes the Camino as a work of archaeology.

“There’s no way to be honest with it without looking at the impacts of colonization, and looking at what happened to the tribes,” he says.

There is personal pain, here, too. Around the circle, people take turns sharing who they are “keeping in their heart” as they walk. For some, it’s a loved one who died or a parent with Alzheimer’s disease. One person mentions a loyal dog who died, another is walking for a sedentary brother who chooses not to exercise. Franklin teaches us to say “Oh!” in unison after each person shares, a solemn chant of recognition to be repeated hundreds of times over the next six days.

Once we get out on the Camino, strolling through suburbia toward Boyes Hot Springs, different pairings and groups take shape. There’s a mother-son team embarking on a “trip of a lifetime,” as Shelly Howe puts it. A veteran of multiple marathons and Iron Man competitions, she’s a seamstress. Her son Clark, 21, is a welder who fabricates winery signs and is by far the youngest in the group. Sam and Marcie Mills are a married couple from Cloverdale. Longtime friends Jo Arney and Robin Wendlandt flew from Portland. Wendlandt has walked over 1,600 miles along different legs of the Camino de Santiago in Spain.

Another pair of friends, Liz Olsen and Bridget Gray, drove from Sacramento. “I came in cold turkey,” says Olsen, explaining she was “in crisis” when Gray told her, “You need a Camino.”

It sounded therapeutic, like the way someone might say you need an Advil or a shot of whiskey, so Olsen agreed to come. “I don’t know what I’m doing,” she says, “But I’m all in.”

This morning, she’s walking for her black Labrador Gemma, who died in her arms after suffering a heart attack on a hilly trail. Also in her heart is her mother-in-law who died in February.

Other returning pilgrims are dropping in for a stage or two. Franklin Jr. is walking just the first stage, sharing tribal lore along with his personal history of overcoming gang life and drug addiction.

At 69, Olga Barnes has completed the Camino seven times. When the Petaluma resident reaches the tenth, she plans to celebrate with a tattoo of the Camino logo on her leg.

Adelina Aramburo, a retired San Francisco kindergarten teacher, finished stage 6 in February, two months after her husband of 39 years died of leukemia. She says she’s still touched by Peacocke’s words to her on that last day. “Adam said, ‘We prayed for you. We know about your trials.’ It was just very gentle, and it just really opened me up.” She temporarily placed her husband’s memorial card in the chapel at Fort Ross. “He was of Russian descent, a Russian Jew, so it felt like he had come full circle.”

Retired Sebastopol electronics and software engineer John Foley is walking the Camino de Sonoma for the first time. He has traveled all over the world, hiking parts of the Camino de Santiago and taking remote journeys in Papua New Guinea, Africa, and Indonesia. At lunch, he says he feels something powerful taking shape here. “It’s like a living thing—all those people walking the same trail have imbued it with an undeniable energy and you can’t help but tap into that.”

One of the first things to know about the Camino is the terminology: The acronym “OCD” stands for “Obsessive Camino Disorder,” describing the intrepid trekkers who find the experience so invigorating they return many times over. In the beginning, it’s said you’re getting your “Camino legs,” and by the end you’re soaring on “Camino wings.”

“Camino coincidences” crop up in the unlikeliest of moments, like when two people walking on the same day discover they’re both there to commemorate a late parent’s 107th birthday. At the slightest hint of serendipity, pilgrims will say, “The Camino provides” in a zen-like cadence that hangs in the air like “the Dude abides” in the cult film “The Big Lebowski.”

The earliest religious pilgrimages to the Holy Land predate written history, going back to the dawn of organized religion. Every year, spiritual pilgrims retrace well-worn paths all around the world, testing their physical endurance along the Camino de Santiago in Europe, Abraham’s Path in the Middle East, Kumano Kodo in Japan, and the Inca Trail in Peru.

In 2017, during a transitional period of his life, Peacocke set out on a walkabout while on a trip to New Zealand where his wife was born. Learning about the rich history of the land and the Maori people had a profound effect on him. “I went 6,000 miles away from home to get inspired about how we might be able to meaningfully engage the beauty and the story of Sonoma County,” he says.

Back home, he pitched the idea to longtime friend McCormick, known to most these days as “Tony Camino.” More than a decade before, they had founded the nonprofit Hope Works to help people who have been incarcerated find meaningful employment after prison. Born in Texas, McCormick grew up in Southern California where his family often camped with no tents, sleeping under the stars. After more than 30 years as an electrician for Hewlett-Packard, he retired and was ready to walk the earth.

The two began hiking all over Sonoma County, trying to connect a network of trails and stories from Sonoma to Fort Ross, until one day in 2019, they found the missing piece in what is now Stage 6. “We stopped at these two cypress trees, and just looked at each other, and we said, ‘This is tangible,’ McCormick remembers. “And we just started crying. We just got overwhelmed.”

Not long after, 11 pilgrims hiked the first Camino de Sonoma. Today, around 650 people have traveled the route. They expect to hit 100 million steps along the path next year. Pilgrims pay nothing to walk the Camino; the endeavor is funded entirely by donations and guides are volunteers.

There is an element of Christian spirituality to the pilgrimage. Peacocke and McCormick often talk about “walking with intention along the healing path.” Each stage is curated with scripture and inspirational quotes read from a pamphlet they pass out to pilgrims, but they make it clear no one needs to subscribe to their beliefs in order to walk.

Clark Howe, the 21-year-old welder, didn’t grow up going to church and isn’t religious. “It’s never really been my sort of thing,” he says. “But the way that they approach it, it’s not in your face. They say, ‘Here’s what’s important to us, and I think you might take something from it.’”

Volunteer guide Christine Matsumoto-Deveaux is a practicing Buddhist and has seen all walks of life set foot on the trail. “A pilgrim is someone who’s in search of finding what they need at that time in their life, whether it be spirituality or not. That’s actually the beauty of the Camino—we don’t care what faith you are,” she says. “You’re one of us, we’re a family, and everyone is here for a different reason.”

Over the next four days, hikers send texts and photos as they walk through Santa Rosa, Sebastopol, Occidental, and beyond. They stop at a backroad lemonade stand, buying up every ounce of juice much to the surprise of the two young kids running it. Shelly Howe sends photos of the group pouring water from their canteens into Willow Creek near Occidental, a trickle they will reunite with as it flows into the Russian River and the Pacific Ocean at Jenner.

“Fatigue on the feet is real at this point,” she writes after Stage 4. “A lot of hills ahead, but we’ve got this! The group is strong for sure!”

Foley, the retired Sebastopol engineer, was only planning to do Stage 1, but he enjoyed the first day so much, he committed to seeing it through to Fort Ross. On the Sebastopol-Occidental leg, his artist son, Owen Foley, met the group at Analy High School where he painted the Japanese internment camp mural and shared his inspiration and creative process with them. For everyone, it’s the highlight of Stage 4.

By the dawn of day six, the eight pilgrims who have been on the trail since Stage 1 are all exhausted, nursing blisters, sore arches, and stiff muscles. Huddled in the Jenner Visitor’s Center parking lot at daybreak, they’re excited to set out for Fort Ross more than 13 miles up the coast.

Along the trail, Clark Howe found a lucky golf ball he’s been using to massage his feet. His mother, Shelly, has been promoted to the role of guide today, an honor that brings tears to her eyes. Several new faces have joined the group. One, wearing a floppy white sun hat, is John Dickinson. He’s celebrating his 80th birthday, four years after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. His devoted wife, Sally Denman, helps him navigate every step. More than a year ago, the longtime Petaluma residents first set foot on the Camino, tackling it stage by stage, and today is their final leg.

As we gather in a circle, Dickinson tells the group how he “appreciates being with you, and talking with you, and learning your stories.” His wife shares how she’s “really grateful our bodies can still do this.”

Everyone chimes “Oh!” in perfect unison, a trail-worn harmony earned over the past five days.

We find a back gate into Jenner Headlands Preserve and wind our way uphill, stopping one-by-one to peek into a shady sanctuary of trees surrounding an outcropping of rocks. A few miles in, Dickinson falls behind. By the time we reach Russian Gulch, he is suffering from heat exhaustion. When the photographer documenting this story arrives, Tony Camino asks if she can give Dickinson a ride to the lunch stop a few miles up the road. The photographer is now “a certified trail angel,” says Matsumoto-Deveaux.

With her husband safe in an air-conditioned car, Denman pushes onward. “The path provided,” she says. “John was offered a ride.”

Next, we navigate a narrow, canopied trail, ringed with poison oak, nicknamed the Hobbit Hole. As it opens into a golden coastal prairie, we arrive at the base of Billy Goat Hill.

Several hundred feet above, truck engines roar along Highway 1 near Sonoma Coast Overlook Park, where we’re headed. Below us, the spell of waves in a blue abyss.

“This is not a race,” Peacocke warns. “So find your pace that works for you.”

This is where Olga Barnes wept uncontrollably the first time she faced the sheer incline; where Steven the Elder wanted to die; and where volunteer Matsumoto-Deveaux repressed the memory of a climb so treacherous that she forgot it existed on her second trek.

Denman digs her hiking boots into the dusty earth. It’s not so much a trail as a series of tiny divots cut into the hillside by deer hooves. She slips, but regains her footing and tells me she and her husband are “Christian and Buddhist, and everything in between.” Between breaths, I ask her why suffering is such an integral part of spirituality around the world. The key to both the Camino and to life, she explains, is “to be open to holding joy and pain in the same moment.”

Stopping to catch our breath at the top, we stumble onto a stakeout, as a pair of state Fish and Wildlife officers hide behind camouflage cover, taking photos of a pair of suspected mussel poachers hauling out heavy bags filled with bivalves, likely well beyond the 10-pound limit. It gives truth to the trail adage, “No two Caminos are ever the same.”

For the next few miles, we teeter on the edge of the narrow highway, guardrails offering the only protection between radiant-hot asphalt and a 300-foot drop. Our guides wave orange flags to warn drivers along the stretch of windy road, which includes crossing a cattle guard, giving new meaning to “walking with intention.” Dickinson, who rejoined the group after lunch, falls behind again, and gets another ride, this time to the finish line.

When we finally arrive at Sandy Cove at Fort Ross, Peacocke is there to high-five every pilgrim at the bottom of the stairs, greeting us with “Welcome to Metini,” an acknowledgment of the original Kashia Pomo village that existed long before the Russians arrived. As the group walks through the replica wooden gate of Fort Ross, it feels like a scene out of “The Amazing Race” reality TV show. Walking up to the chapel, Shelly Howe and her son Clark can’t hold back the tears. “I told myself I wasn’t gonna do this!” he says. His mom is so choked up, she can hardly talk.

Many take off their well-worn shoes and stretch out in the sand. Clark and his father, Darren, who joined the last two stages, splash in the cold Pacific waters. We gather for a closing ceremony, and everyone who completed all six stages receives a ceremonial purple cord. A slow grin spreads across John Dickinson’s face as he receives his symbolic string. It reminds me of something his wife said halfway up Billy Goat Hill: “You need to grab everything in life, because tomorrow is never promised.”

Everyone shares a final thought punctuated by the group’s conclusive, resonant “Oh!” After taking turns ringing the chapel bell, there are refreshments, then they go their separate ways, but not before sharing hugs, phone numbers, and new text chains.

“Let’s do the Camino de Santiago next year!” Robin Wendlandt tells Shelly Howe.

A few days later, Howe sends a text after uploading trail data from her watch. A total of 85.2 miles, 25 hours of walking, and a total elevation gain of 8,353 feet—2,500 of those on the final day. Impressive numbers, to be sure, but they’re only part of the story. “If we let the Camino bring us what we need, we will find it. I did find it,” she writes, confirming one of the mantras repeated along the miles.

The Camino provides.

The post The Camino de Sonoma Offers Hikers a Physical and Spiritual Journey appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Wylde Provisions Co. Lets Parents Linger While the Kids Run Wild
summary:
Wylde Provisions Co. in Sebastopol gives parents a place to linger over espresso, beer and protein-packed meals while the kids run wild.

The post Wylde Provisions Co. Lets Parents Linger While the Kids Run Wild appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
I didn’t plan to write about an organic, gluten-free oat pancake served on a paper plate and smeared with peanut-free nut butter. But here I am, stuffing the last sticky bite into my mouth. It’s surprisingly good for something from a kids’ menu.

Small children are screaming, running and jumping around me, which makes sense, considering I’m in their world: a playground in the middle of Sebastopol. Around me is an assortment of millennial parents who look tired but happy to have a place where they can sit in the shade with a proper espresso — or beer — and eat a chef-made tofu soba noodle bowl while their children run wild at Wylde Provisions Co.

All I can think about is how good everything tastes: the yogurt parfait with blueberry coulis, the soba noodles and a giant carnitas sandwich with refried lentils and tomatillo-fish sauce vinaigrette.

At a playground. In Sebastopol. With toddlers everywhere.

Wylde Provisions Co. is one of those “Why didn’t I think of that?” ideas. It comes from firefighter, paramedic and gym owner Urban Anderson and chef Andrew Truong of Terrapin Creek restaurant. The unlikely partners bonded over a shared idea: healthy, protein-forward food that was affordable and portable.

“Food is medicine. What you put into your body is what you’re going to put back into the world,” Anderson said.

Building one bowl at a time

Their first effort was a refrigerator at Anderson’s gym, The Barn Fitness Collective, stocked with chef-made grain bowls packed with macro-friendly ingredients such as curried chicken breast, pickled vegetables, edamame and arugula.

Because the sauce is everything, Truong developed tzatziki yogurt, miso-sesame, red curry-peanut and avocado-lime-cilantro sauces to wake up the bowls.

But as orders came in at a steady clip, they quickly ran out of prep space at Truong’s restaurant. They needed a commissary kitchen and found one at St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church in a space that had previously housed a small church cafe.

With walk-up windows and an outdoor play area, it seemed ideal for both a commissary and a much-needed family-friendly gathering place. Anderson’s son, Wylder — the cafe’s namesake — was the first tester, heading straight for the slide while his father inspected the kitchen.

The cafe has since expanded its offerings to include bigger eats such as meatballs and sandwiches, as well as happy-hour specials like deviled eggs. There’s also coffee, snacks, beer, nonalcoholic bubbles and prebiotic sodas.

Win-win.

New bowls drop Mondays and Thursdays, when service is grab-and-go only. This week’s offering was Berberian Rhapsody — they all have clever names — with Ethiopian-inspired, berbere-spiced chicken or tofu, black lentils, farro, pickled peppers, garlicky collard greens, roasted cauliflower and preserved-lemon vinaigrette. It packs 46 grams of protein into 544 calories.

Past creations have included the Tamariana Grande, with tamari-glazed turkey sausage over udon with edamame, charred zucchini, pickled ginger and cashew-tamari vinaigrette, and the Chipotle Off the Old Block, with chipotle chicken or tofu, quinoa, black beans, corn and greens tossed in avocado-cilantro dressing.

Executive chef Nick Cobarruvias makes the kind of food you can eat every day and feel both good and smug about. There’s plenty of protein and a lot of vegetables, but none of the earnestness that can make “healthy” food feel like homework.

The details

Fridays through Sundays, Wylde Provisions Co. offers an expanded menu featuring sandwiches and happy-hour specials from 4:30-5:30 p.m., along with live music.

Anderson and Truong are now expanding the business through new sales channels, including smart vending machines and corporate delivery.

“Our objective is to create a regional health food brand,” Anderson said.

All ages are welcome, though weekend evenings tend to be the most adult-friendly. The kids’ menu includes chicken nuggets, grilled cheese and, of course, the peanut-free nut butter pancake. Because when it comes to pancakes, we’re all kids at heart.

Wylde Provisions Co. is at 500 Robinson Road, Sebastopol. For more information, visit wyldeprovisions.com/playground-cafe. Weekly bowl drops are announced on Instagram at @wyldeprovisionsco.

title: Inside The Porch Kitchen, a Tucked-Away West County Favorite
summary:
Easy to miss but worth finding, The Porch Kitchen is a tucked-away French bistro near The Barlow where chef Lisa Boisset serves scratch-made classics without the fuss.

The post Inside The Porch Kitchen, a Tucked-Away West County Favorite appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Chef Lisa Boisset is obsessive about making nearly everything at her tiny Sebastopol bistro from scratch. Stocks and sauces, dressings and focaccia croutons — the longtime caterer and classically trained French chef can’t imagine doing it any other way.

At her recently opened Porch Kitchen, even the ketchup requires a multistep process: tomatoes are charred, then simmered with warm spices, apple cider vinegar and balsamic vinegar. That kind of condiment commitment outside a three-Michelin-star restaurant can feel a little precious, because, let’s be honest, most people are perfectly happy with Heinz.

I’m reconsidering.

Boisset’s ketchup turns her Parmesan- and parsley-topped pomme frites into a hand-slapping, finger-licking scramble for the last bite.

“I don’t want to serve it if I can’t make it from scratch,” Boisset said, putting a fine point on a philosophy that’s run through her career.

A graduate of Le Cordon Bleu in Paris and a veteran of several Michelin-starred restaurants, Boisset has spent much of her professional life cooking through her catering company, The Cook & The Drummer, which she started with her husband, Kevin, in 2011. She knows what works. And what doesn’t.

Back to the table

Restaurant life was one thing that stopped working when Boisset became a mother. The grueling nighttime hours led her to catering, allowing her to keep cooking professionally while spending more time with her family.

Fifteen years later, she found herself drawn back to the restaurant kitchen.

“I wasn’t planning this, and it was a bit courageous and daring, but I felt like Sebastopol needed a little bistro like this,” she said.

Boisset is once again cooking the traditional French food she loved as a young chef, drawing inspiration from “Larousse Gastronomique” and Auguste Escoffier. The approach is classical without being fussy, and it seems to be resonating with the neighborhood.

“I’m not trying to reinvent the wheel here. It’s just a humble brasserie,” she said. “Something a little different for Sebastopol, and from my heart.”

The spot

The Porch Kitchen sits a pommes frites throw from The Barlow, tucked beside Patisserie Angelica and behind the Rialto Cinemas. Neither spot is especially visible from the main drag, which has helped make them local favorites while leaving them easy for outsiders to miss.

The space, a former barbecue restaurant that most recently housed Goatlandia Kitchen, is decidedly not white-tablecloth – or tablecloth at all. The open-air porch has a roadhouse feel, while the patio’s simple, umbrella-shaded picnic tables are more Sonoma west county than Paris Left Bank.

Boisset and her husband run most of the show, with help from a small staff of servers and cooks. During the day, the restaurant primarily operates as a grab-and-go cafe, though table service is available. In the evenings, an intimate happy hour and dinner service have quickly gained traction through word of mouth.

Kevin, a jazz drummer by trade, doubles as the bistro’s sommelier and host. The wine list leans toward affordable bottles from his native France, along with selections from Sonoma Coast and Dry Creek Valley wineries.

The daytime menu focuses on craveable salads, sandwiches and grain bowls. At night, Boisset stretches her classical French muscles with bistro standards, including salade lyonnaise, ratatouille, roasted chicken and crème brûlée.

The food is simple and comforting, without pretense or ego. Like any good caterer, Boisset keeps the focus on the food and the guest rather than the work happening behind the scenes.

But that, in part, is what makes The Porch Kitchen worth seeking out – everything is made from scratch, including the ketchup.

Best bets

Melted Normandy Delight, $22: Boisset takes melted cheese to another level with an earthy, washed-rind cheese from Marin French Cheese Company. Bathed in flambéed French cider and topped with warm-spiced apple compote and thyme chutney, it arrives molten and fragrant with crisp focaccia crackers on the side. Christmas on a plate, any time of year.

Pommes frites, $12: Yes, the fries are excellent — and one of the few things Boisset doesn’t make from scratch, because even she has limits. But the housemade ketchup and garlicky aioli turn them into a table brawl over the last few crumbs.

Brussels sprouts with candied pecans, $14: Even Brussels sprouts skeptics can get behind these tiny cruciferous nuggets, studded with bacon and candied pecans and drizzled with lemon aioli. I’ll die on that hill.

Salade Lyonnaise, $18: A classic for a reason. Fresh frisée gets a generous dousing of warm vinaigrette and plenty of bacon lardons. Salads don’t have to be good for you.

Orange, fennel and beet salad, $18: Wine Country seems determined to put a beet salad on every menu, but this version gets it right. Lightly pickled beets mingle with butter lettuce, fennel, pea shoots, crumbled goat cheese, flower petals and citrus in a tangy vinaigrette.

Airline chicken breast, $28: Tender breast and thigh come with crisp skin and rosemary-garlic jus reduced to a flavor-packed syrup. Herb-roasted potatoes and baby carrots round out the plate. It puts Ina Garten’s holy-grail roast chicken in a corner.

Ratatouille, $22: This iconic Provençal dish shows just how obsessive Boisset can be, with perfect coins of zucchini, eggplant and tomato arranged in concentric circles in a French ramekin. It’s almost too pretty to eat. An herb-infused red pepper sauce adds a bit of Wine Country flair that isn’t strictly French but works beautifully.

Pan-seared wild salmon, $36: The salmon is delightful, but the real showstopper is the combination of buttery potato mousseline and citrus beurre blanc. It’s butter-on-butter ridiculousness.

Crème brûlée, $14: No notes. Just yes.

Happy hour

Beef sliders, $12: Happy little dry-aged burgers topped with caramelized onion jam. Tiny but mighty two-biters.

Salmon cakes, $14: I’m over crab cakes and their outrageous prices. Made with fresh salmon trim, these are tastier and more satisfying, especially sitting in a puddle of creamy remoulade. Take that, tired old tartar sauce.

Mac and cheese, $9: Four cheeses devoured by four forks. Breadcrumbs and ramekin left spinning empty on the table.

Hibiscus mint tea, $5: My go-to refresher every time I’m there. I’m considering asking for a punch card next time.

The Porch Kitchen is open for lunch from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Dinner is from 5:30-8 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday, with happy hour from 3-5:30 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday. Reservations are highly recommended. 6811 Laguna Park Way, Sebastopol, 707-494-0996, theporchkitchen.com

title: 33 Best Dog-Friendly Wineries in Sonoma County
summary:
Get ready for Yappy Hour! These Sonoma County wineries welcome pooches and their wine-loving parents.

The post 33 Best Dog-Friendly Wineries in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Sonoma County, with its many renowned vineyards, is a great place to enjoy a day of wine tasting. The region is also a great place for dogs and their owners, with an increasing number of parks, establishments and venues welcoming and catering to canine companions.

But just where should you go if you want to visit a winery while also spending time with your furry best friend? Fortunately, there are plenty of options in the county — and some of them have special events planned for this year’s International Dog Day, Aug. 26.

Sonoma

Gundlach Bundschu Winery

One of the oldest wineries in California welcomes on-leash dogs to their Rhinefarm. Enjoy a wine tasting with seasonal snacks on the courtyard patio, which overlooks the estate vineyards, or bring your dog into the historic tasting room, a pet-friendly pick for a rainy day. 2000 Denmark St., 707-938-5277, gunbun.com

Larson Family Winery

Larson Family Winery makes a dog-themed wine, Three Lab Cab, named after former winery dogs Buster, Bubba and Pete. Current resident winery dogs will also greet guests to the tasting room. Dogs are welcome (on a leash) on the lawn and picnic area, where you can play cornhole while your dog relaxes in the sun. 23355 Millerick Road, 707-938-3031, larsonfamilywinery.com 

Bartholomew Estate Vineyards and Winery

Located within 375-acre Bartholomew Park in Sonoma Valley, Bartholomew winery has a variety of great views and trails for humans and canines to enjoy. Leashes are required at all times. 1000 Vineyard Lane, 707-509-0540, bartholomewestate.com

Roche Winery

Watch the world go by, dog by your side, on the patio of this downtown tasting room, with a fire pit and trees providing shade. The tasting room offers barrel tastings, snacks and some of the best people-watching in town. 122 W. Spain St., 707-935-7115, rochewinery.com

Anaba Wines

Anaba loves its dog guests so much that it treats them to complimentary, chef-made dog cookies. A bowl of dog-friendly “Char-Dog-Nay” is available for purchase off the tasting menu, so guests and their pups can sip in style. Pets must remain close and well-supervised at all times. 62 Bonneau Road, Sonoma, 707-996-4188, anabawines.com

Glen Ellen

B.R. Cohn Winery

This Glen Ellen winery offers water bowls and treats for visiting dogs to enjoy. Leashed dogs are welcome on the winery patio and grounds, which include estate vineyards and views of Sonoma and the Mayacamas mountains. 15000 Sonoma Highway, 707-938-4064, brcohn.com

Mayo Family Winery

Mayo’s Glen Ellen tasting room is dog-friendly and open for tastings daily. Guests can also bring a picnic and their pets to the outdoor courtyard. 13101 Arnold Drive, Glen Ellen, 707-938-9401, mayofamilywinery.com

Kenwood

Deerfield Ranch Winery

“May All Fours Be With You” is the motto of Deerfield Ranch’s winery dog, Obi Wine Kenobi. Water is available for pooches, while dog owners can taste some of the wineries delectable vintages. 10200 Sonoma Highway, 707-833-5215, deerfieldranch.com

Kunde Family Winery

Fourth-generation winegrower Jeff Kunde invites well-behaved, leashed dogs to the estate’s Kinneybrook patio and 202 Lounge bar, where tastings take place daily. 9825 Sonoma Highway, 707-833-5501, kunde.com

Landmark Vineyards

Well-behaved, leashed dogs are welcome to wander with their owners on the outdoor property. Thirsty dogs get a taste of the royal treatment: Fiji water fresh from the bottle served in a bowl. 101 Adobe Canyon Road, 707-833-0053, landmarkwine.com

Muscardini Cellars

Winemaker Michael Muscardini’s golden retriever, Biondi, and staff welcome well-behaved, leashed dogs in the tasting room and on the patio and green rolling grounds behind the tasting room. Dogs can look forward to treats, water and toys as well as dog-themed events. 9380 Sonoma Highway, 707-933-9305, muscardinicellars.com

Santa Rosa

Balletto Vineyards

The family-owned winery says it usually has dog treats and water bowls at the ready for visiting dogs. Just make sure your dog is on a leash during the entire visit. 5700 Occidental Road, 707-568-2455, ballettovineyards.com

Belden Barns

This family-run winery prides itself on being dog-friendly and kid-friendly. The property, which is located on Sonoma Mountain, is also a working farm that produces a diverse array of fruits and vegetables. 5561 Sonoma Mountain Road, 415-577-8552, beldenbarns.com

Matanzas Creek Winery

Well-behaved dogs on a leash are welcome outside at Matanzas Creek, where aromatic lavender gardens line the property. 6097 Bennett Valley Road, 707-521-7019, matanzascreek.com

St. Francis Winery

Named after St. Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals and the environment, this Santa Rosa winery lives up to its namesake by supporting local animal charities and partnering with Canine Companions, to which it has contributed over $400,000 since 2021. Friendly pets are welcome on the property and must be leashed at all times. The winery will host its annual Blessing of the Animals Fundraiser from 2-5 p.m., Oct. 4, in support of local animal rescue nonprofits. Admission is free but donations are welcome. There will be wine by the glass as well as a raffle and Winery Dog of the Year contest. 100 Pythian Road, Santa Rosa, 707-833-0242, stfranciswinery.com

Windsor

Mutt Lynch Winery

Winemaker Brenda Lynch’s winery is both an ode to wine and to furry friends. The tasting room hosts “Yappy Hour” events and offers water, treats, toys and possible playmates, as staff members often bring their pups to work. The winery also raises funds for animal rescue organizations through its Wines That Give Back program. 9050 Windsor Road, 707-687-5089, muttlynchwinery.com

Bricoleur Vineyards

Bricoleur’s Essentials Picnic tasting ($75 per tasting flight) is the perfect excuse to treat yourself and your furry friend to an alfresco lunch by the estate pond with a glass of refreshing sparkling wine. Dogs are welcome in all outdoor areas at Bricoleur Vineyards, as well as indoors to join their owners during tastings. All dogs should be leashed and never left unattended. 7394 Starr Road, 707-857-5700, bricoleurvineyards.com

Martinelli Winery

The historic Martinelli Winery & Vineyards welcomes well-behaved dogs on a leash for its Vineyard Terrace Tasting ($50 per person). The tasting includes a flight of estate wines to sip on the terrace overlooking the Hop Barn Hill Vineyard, with the option to add a picnic lunch and bottle service. Only service animals are allowed inside the tasting room. 3360 River Road, 707-525-0570, martinelliwinery.com

La Crema

Located within Saralee’s Vineyard in the Russian River Valley, La Crema Estate also welcomes dogs. The site’s landmark historic barn has been converted into a tasting room and wine education facility. Dogs should be on a leash at all times. 3575 Slusser Road, 707-525-6200, lacrema.com

Two Shepherds

Named for the owners’ two Australian shepherds, Arya and Austin, Two Shepherds winery is not only pet friendly — animals are a part of the whole operation. Donkeys help turn the soil in the wintertime, the estate cats hunt for gophers in the vineyards and the dogs serve as friendly brand ambassadors. There are even wines named after some of Two Shepherds’ furry family, like the “Wiley” Carbonic Carignan named after cat Wiley and the “L’il Trouble” Mourvèdre named after their frisky Nigerian dwarf goat Trouble. The winery also releases a canned sparkling orange wine called “Natty Pets,” which features the furry farm crew on its colorful label. 7763 Bell Road, Windsor, 415-613-5731, twoshepherds.com

Healdsburg

Amista Vineyards

Guests can bring their leashed, four-legged companions to this dog-friendly Healdsburg winery, where they can enjoy a walk on a half-mile path through the vineyards. The covered, solar-paneled patio is an idyllic place to relax with the pup and enjoy a wine tasting with stunning views. Amista staff will provide water bowls and dog biscuits. Bonus: You may even get to meet the winery’s own shelties. 3320 Dry Creek Road, 707-431-9200, amistavineyards.com

Bacchus Landing

With a reputation of being “super” dog friendly, this collective of just over a half dozen boutique wineries is a hub of winemaking and tasting activity. Bacchus Landing is equally family-friendly with bocce courts and lawn games as well as a large open patio and five tasting rooms, among them Smith Story Wine Cellars and resident goldendoodle Sir Royal Soup, brother to the late social media-sensation Lord Sandwich. 14210 Bacchus Landing Way, 707-395-0697, bacchuslanding.com

Breathless Wines

Guests can enjoy a flight of sparkling wines on the winery’s garden patio accompanied by their dogs. The winery also hosts fundraisers for Humane Society of Sonoma County. Out of courtesy for other visitors and staff, the winery requests that all animals are leashed and well-behaved. 499 Moore Lane, 707-395-7300, breathlesswines.com

Lambert Bridge Winery

This Healdsburg winery allows dogs to settle into a dog bed and relax with a bowl of water while owners sip some wines. After enjoying a tasting, wander through the estate gardens with your pup. Dogs should remain leashed throughout the visit and bag dispensers are available near the garden entrance for guests to pick up after their dogs. 4085 W. Dry Creek Road, 707-431-9600, lambertbridge.com

Portalupi Wine

This winery’s downtown tasting room is a convenient stop along a dog walk. The family is a supporter of the local Humane Society and donates proceeds from their wine sales to the nonprofit. 107 North St., 707-395-0960, portalupiwine.com

West Wines

The winery, with a tasting room below a large oak with views of the vineyards, invites guests to enjoy a tasting on the dog-friendly patio. West Wines’ Instagram account occasionally features an assortment of photos of some of its canine visitors as well as its “winery cat extraordinaire” Jane Bond. 1000 Dry Creek Road, 707-433-2066, westwines.com

Wilson Winery

The Wilsons make a dog-themed wine, Three Dog Zin, which features the family’s three dogs, Molly, Sydney and Victoria. The staff welcomes well-behaved, leashed dogs, offering pups treats and water, while humans sip Zinfandel in the tasting room or on the patio overlooking the vineyards. 1960 Dry Creek Road, 707-433-4355, wilsonwinery.com

Cloverdale

BobDog Wines

Named after a beloved Rottweiler that lived at Sky Pine Vineyards over 20 years ago, BobDog Wines lives up to its reputation as a dog-friendly winery, where pets are free to walk around on a leash. A portion of wine sales proceeds benefit programs for the protection and care of animals. 31955 Pine Mountain Road, 707-756-2471, bobdogwine.com

Geyserville

Dutcher Crossing Winery

Dogs are welcome in the tasting room, where they can wear winery-branded dog collars available for purchase while their owners taste estate Zinfandel and other small-production wines. The back patio and lawn is a great spot for nibbling on cheese and charcuterie, and playing catch. 8533 Dry Creek Road, 707-431-2700, dutchercrossingwinery.com

Sebastopol

Dutton-Goldfield Winery

Canine companions are celebrated at the winery, with special dog cookies offered to pets. Winery partner Theresa Dutton serves on the Northwest regional board of Canine Companions for Independence, a nonprofit that provides service and therapy dogs to those in need. 3100 Gravenstein Highway N., 707-823-3887, duttongoldfield.com

Horse & Plow

Located in a historic Sebastopol barn near local vineyards and apple orchards, Horse & Plow welcomes well-behaved dogs and their owners to the tasting room. Treats and water are provided to pups. Dogs must remain on a leash at all times. 1272 Gravenstein Highway N., 707-827-3486, horseandplow.com

Marimar Estate Vineyards and Winery

This winery and vineyard, owned and operated by the Spanish-American Torres family, welcomes well-behaved dogs on a leash on the property. Visitors will also find some larger than life dogs on the winery grounds — 10-foot metal sculptures of the owners’ springer spaniels, Chico and Bonita. 11400 Graton Road, 707-823-4365, marimarestate.com

Taft Street Winery

Taft Street Winery is a family-friendly business — and that includes dogs. Well-behaved pups on a leash are welcome on the winery’s back patio. The winery also provides treats and water bowls. 2030 Barlow Lane, 707-823-2049, taftstreetwinery.com

Sarah Stierch and Maci Martell contributed to this article.

The post 33 Best Dog-Friendly Wineries in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Flora Springs Wine Lounge Brings Wine Cocktails and Roman-Inspired Glamour to Downtown Napa
summary:
The new Napa tasting room pairs wines with lighter-style cocktails, fresh botanicals and a lavish setting inspired by the Roman goddess of flowers.

The post Flora Springs Wine Lounge Brings Wine Cocktails and Roman-Inspired Glamour to Downtown Napa appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
There are nearly two dozen winery tasting rooms in downtown Napa, but few are quite like Flora Springs Wine Lounge. With sumptuous, playful décor inspired by Roman and Greek mythology, the venue shakes things up with cocktails made from Flora Springs wines, sparkling cuvées and fresh botanicals.

The story

For years, Wine Country power couple Jean-Charles Boisset and Gina Gallo have acquired and transformed historic California wineries, including Buena Vista Winery in Sonoma and Raymond Vineyards in Napa.

Even as many large wine companies shed brands amid a prolonged industry downturn, Boisset and Gallo continue to expand. The couple added Flora Springs Winery to their collection in 2024 and later began a dramatic renovation of the original St. Helena winery, founded in 1978 by the Komes family. In March, while construction was underway, they opened the Flora Springs Wine Lounge in downtown Napa.

“People are saying it’s the end of the wine world,” Boisset said of the current industry climate. “I say, not at all. I’m actually more excited than ever. People are drinking less, but more cleverly.”

He says consumers are also gravitating toward lighter-style wines with lower alcohol levels, including wine-based cocktails.

At Flora Springs Wine Lounge, guests can taste serious, vineyard-designated Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignons or opt for a spritzy drink made with sparkling wine and Sauvignon Blanc.

“We wanted to provide an alternative experience [in downtown Napa],” Boisset said, describing his vision for a fun, relaxed space filled with beauty. “We want to capture people’s attention, invite them to dream with us and to go into an escape.”

The vibe

A major element of what Boisset calls the “reincarnation” of the Flora Springs brand story is a focus on Flora, the Roman goddess of flowers, spring and fertility. The winery was originally named for Flora Komes, the Komes family matriarch.

You won’t find any of Boisset’s signature leopard print here. Instead, Flora Springs Wine Lounge is dripping in Baccarat chandeliers and deep green upholstery, with the sort of theatrical glamour that might entice Flora and Botticelli’s Venus — depicted together in a large framed artwork near the entrance — to swing by for a few drinks among the mortals.

The centerpiece of the main-floor salon is a marble bar inset with luminous green and blue accents. Boisset says the design evokes the Napa Valley landscape and the cycle of the seasons.

At the top of a grand staircase, a hidden mezzanine invites guests to settle into plush midnight-blue banquettes beneath dramatic celestial artwork.

On the palate

The lounge offers Flora Springs wines by the glass, flight and bottle, alongside wine-based cocktails. Under Boisset and Gallo’s ownership, the winery continues to produce many of the classic Napa Valley wines that put Flora Springs on the map, along with newer additions such as Vermentino.

The 2023 Napa Valley Trilogy ($115), a Bordeaux-style blend, is built to last, with balanced notes of cigar-box spice and blackberry. The 2024 Napa Valley Soliloquy ($90), a blend of Sauvignon Blanc, Malvasia and Vermentino, has lovely floral aromas and peachy-citrus flavors.

More than 25 wines are available by the glass, starting at $13. Flights range from $40 for a selection of whites to $125 for a focused tasting of single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon.

On the cocktail side, the Napa 75 ($17) is a lighter take on the French 75, combining Sauvignon Blanc, lemon, honey and JCB Brut sparkling wine. For something more herbal, try the Ruby Negroni Sbagliato ($19), a blend of Pinot Noir, bitter botanicals, blood orange and sparkling wine.

The lounge also offers artisan cheese and charcuterie, caviar service and wine-infused chocolate truffles.

Beyond the bottle

In January, Boisset launched another kind of sensory experience with longtime wine educator Ashley Pengilly. Located in First Street Napa Plaza beneath the Archer Hotel, Napa Fragrance sells subtly scented room sprays, candles and hand soaps inspired by Napa Valley growing regions.

The products are made with plant-based, organic ingredients. Guests can also book a guided experience to explore curated scent compositions and blend a custom home fragrance.

Flora Springs Wine Lounge, 1142 First St., Napa. Open from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. Wednesdays, Thursdays and Sundays; from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays. florasprings.com

Tina Caputo is a wine, food, and travel writer whose work has appeared in numerous publications, including SevenFifty Daily, Visit California, HuffPost, and Sonoma Magazine. Follow Tina on Bluesky at @winebroad and visit her website at tinacaputo.com.

title: A Healdsburg Artist Preserves Stunning Sonoma County Landscapes on Canvas
summary:
During the 1980s, Healdsburg artist Christopher Leith Evans painted film backgrounds for "Star Wars" and "Indiana Jones." Now, Sonoma County’s landscapes capture his attention.

The post A Healdsburg Artist Preserves Stunning Sonoma County Landscapes on Canvas appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Blue skies are bandied about in song lyrics from artists such as Irving Berlin, Louis Armstrong, and Electric Light Orchestra. They’re the subject of small talk on a cloudless, sun-drenched Sonoma County afternoon.

And then you meet Healdsburg artist Christopher Leith Evans, and realize how inadequate the word “blue” is for describing something as expansive and ever-changing as the sky.

“I’ve spent a lifetime contemplating the color of the sky,” says Evans, who begins each of his light-filled landscape oil paintings with the sky itself. “It gives you a sense of the lighting. Getting that right and getting that smooth is always a challenge.”

In his home studio in a two-story cottage perched above the Russian River, Evans keeps close at hand an array of blue pigments — cerulean, manganese, cobalt, Provence violet, and lapis lazuli, the vibrant hue used by painters of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. He has made countless studies of the sky at different times of day, blending those blues with white, black, yellows, pinks, and greens — a discipline that lends his paintings such startling realism that they can appear photographic at first glance.

Evans’ gift for rendering these scenes so lifelike may be partly instinctive, but it is also the product of long discipline. During the 1980s, he often spent 10-hour days painting film backgrounds for Industrial Light & Magic, the visual effects company founded by George Lucas. “My years working for George Lucas helped me hone my skills for getting color and light really accurate,” says Evans, who worked on films such as “Return of the Jedi,” “E.T.,” and “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom.” He won a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Special Visual Effects for the televised film “The Ewok Adventure” and received an Academy Award nomination for “Willow,” for which he supervised matte paintings including a slow pullback revealing the Russian River in the film’s final scene.

The long hours and peculiar demands of the work eventually wore on him. Matte painting, the process Evans used in films, involves painting scenes on glass while leaving empty spaces for live action. Over time, it led him to a realization: “I have to do paintings that don’t have holes in them.”

A co-worker suggested he open a gallery, and so he quit. “It’s difficult when you have a prestigious, good-paying job and you walk away from it,” he says.

Evans moved to Healdsburg in 1990 and Sonoma County’s landscapes have occupied much of his attention since. As he paints, he meditates not only on color but also on the shapes of rocks and leaves, and the dual nature of water as both a window to the world beneath the surface and a mirror to the life above. “It flips the world upside down, and there’s something beautiful about that,” he says.

From the back deck of his home, a mile or so downstream from the Del Rio Woods Regional Park beach access, the river can sometimes be lively with kayakers, paddle boarders, and tubers drifting through its cool, gentle flow. But early on a weekday morning, with no one in sight except a family of geese gliding below, a Violet-green swallow swooping overhead, and a pair of watchful scrub jays guarding their nest nearby, Evans lowered his voice almost to a whisper. “You can hear the water.”

Painting, for him, engages more than sight. He notices the sound of water rippling over rocks, the calls of birds and even the smell of willows as he ducks beneath them while walking to the river with a French easel strapped to his back to paint en plein air. There, standing calf-deep in the water, he searches for the precise angle from which to capture a cottonwood on the bank upstream and the colors of the late-afternoon sky.

There’s a natural kinship between his art and his environmental sensibility. “As you observe, you think. You become a naturalist and a conservationist,” he says. “When you love something, you want to protect it.”

Evans also paints figurative works. His recent painting, “Artemis Alone at the River of Extinction,” depicting the goddess of the forest gazing into a pool of dying monarch butterflies, offers a quiet reflection on ecological loss. This spring, it received the top prize for social commentary in the Art Renewal Center’s 18th annual Salon Competition, among the world’s most prestigious competitions devoted to realist art, according to its website. The painting appeared in an exhibition and auction at Sotheby’s in New York in July. For Evans, the honor was an unexpected recognition. “It blew my mind when I got that,” he says.

Born on the West Coast and raised in New York, Evans grew up in what he calls “an art-oriented family.” His grandfather, an amateur artist, taught him to paint and draw at an early age. As a teenager, Evans spent hours studying Old Master paintings at The Frick Collection on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, just steps from Central Park. In high school, he made a fateful choice to end his misery in physics and switch to an art class, a change he likens to “throwing an otter into a swimming pool.” He began his studies at the University of California, Los Angeles, as an art history major, considering it the more practical path, but passion prevailed, and he eventually changed to studio art.

Though he loves the outdoors — particularly the trails around Lake Sonoma and Pepperwood Preserve, where he served as artist in residence in 2017 shortly before the Tubbs Fire — Evans says it is more practical to paint indoors. While some of his smaller works are portable, many of his canvases are measured in feet rather than inches.

Even his tools evoke the natural world. He keeps brushes made from sable, boar, and badger hair, favoring badger for blending the colors in his skies. One brush he fashioned himself by attaching a natural sponge to a stick that he uses to paint tree leaves, a technique he learned while working for George Lucas.

Still, Evans spends as much time outside as possible, searching for moments such as when the light and the clouds, the curve of the earth, and the arch of a stately oak seem to harmonize. “I try to capture the overall feeling of the forms as they interrelate to each other,” he says. He paddles stretches of the river by kayak or drives toward the coast in pursuit of shifting clouds. “I’ve earned this kind of freedom. I’m 71. I’ve spent a lot of time in dark rooms, in warehouses, working on movies,” he says. “I feel a little guilty just getting in my car, but I feel like I’ve earned it. And I share it.”

He recently exhibited work at Spring Lake Village in Santa Rosa, and two of his paintings are on view at the Lori Austin Gallery in Healdsburg. Evans also maintains a private viewing space in downtown Healdsburg that’s open by appointment.

“My goal with landscape painting is that people will appreciate what I have appreciated,” he says, comparing his paintings to a window that invites the eye to linger and then wander further.

“I sometimes think of myself as a view farmer,” Evans says. “I’m harvesting and cultivating these beautiful views of nature we have here.”

Find Christopher Leith Evans’ Art

Gallery 433 

Private exhibition space. By appointment only.

707-326-1551, christopherleithevans.com

Lori Austin Gallery

105 Plaza St., Healdsburg

707-395-4661, loriaustingallery.com

The post A Healdsburg Artist Preserves Stunning Sonoma County Landscapes on Canvas appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.

title: Where to Find the Best Waffles in Sonoma County
summary:
No need to travel to Belgium to find delicious waffles. Here's the best of the sweet breakfast treat in Sonoma County.

The post Where to Find the Best Waffles in Sonoma County appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
While the United States celebrates National Waffle Day on Aug. 24, International Waffle Day is held March 25, celebrating the worldwide love of the sweet breakfast food. But the annual foodie holiday reportedly began as a misunderstanding.

First, the origin of the waffle

According to Smithsonian Magazine, the waffle dates back to ancient Greece, where Athenians roasted flat cakes called obelios between two hot metal plates.

Later adapted to the French oublies during the Middle Ages, the edible discs typically depicted Biblical scenes and religious iconography, as they served as a sort of communion wafer, eaten after meals as a symbolic blessing. Made of simple grain flour and water, the food was commonplace among all walks of society throughout Europe by the 13th century.

As cooks gained access to different ingredients and spices, the recipe of the wafer changed over time, transforming into a delicacy called a gaufre or wafel. Eventually, the treat traveled around the world, picking up new names, flavors and designs.

So how did Waffle Day start?

While the first iterations of the waffle gained popularity as a communion wafer, Waffle Day began with a Christian holiday, the Feast of Annunciation or the Day of Our Lady. Typically held on March 25, it commemorates the moment archangel Gabriel told Mary she would give birth to God’s son.

Waffle – the food – has little to do with this celebration but its name, in Swedish, apparently made March 25 the designated day for waffles, all due to a misunderstanding, according to tourism website Visit Sweden. In Sweden, the Feast of Annunciation is called “Vårfrudagen” (the Day of Our Lady), which sounds very similar to “våffeldagen,” which means the waffle day.

Over time, it became tradition to eat waffles on March 25, and soon Waffle Day was celebrated all across Europe. And while the U.S. has its own National Waffle Day on Aug. 24 — coinciding with the patenting of the first American waffle iron in 1869, invented by Cornelius Swarthout of Troy, New York — it doesn’t hurt to celebrate the treat at least twice a year.

A variety of waffles from around the world include the fluffy Brussels-style Belgian waffle; Sweden’s crispy, heart-shaped waffles; the thin, cookie-like Dutch stroopwafels; the fish-shaped Japanese taiyaki waffles; the green Vietnamese pandan waffle; the savory, U.K.-based potato waffles and many more.

No need to travel the world to find a hot plate of delicious waffles. Here’s the best of the sweet breakfast treat in Sonoma County to celebrate International Waffle Day on March 25, America’s National Waffle Day on Aug. 24, or any day of the year.

Favorite Sonoma County waffles

Sunflower Caffe

The rotating seasonal menu currently offers a strawberry shortcake waffle — a buttermilk waffle topped with Watmaugh strawberries, Chantilly cream, shortbread crumble, whipped butter and maple syrup. A gluten-free oat waffle can be subbed for $2. 421 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-996-6645, sonomasunflower.com

Verano Cafe

The Sonoma cafe offers a Belgian buttermilk waffle topped with seasonal fruit, whipped cream and syrup. Or, spring for a classic waffle and fried chicken served with a side of country potatoes. 18976 Sonoma Highway, Sonoma, 707-931-6837, veranocafesonoma.com

Sax’s Joint

This 1950s-style diner has an extensive breakfast menu, including a handful of waffle dishes. Go for the classic chicken and waffles or take it next level with the spicy bacon cheddar waffle. Prefer a sweeter take on the morning treat? Delight your inner child with Baily Shay’s Cereal Waffle. 317 Petaluma Blvd. S., Petaluma, 707-559-3021, saxsjoint.com

Blue Plate

Petaluma’s newest neighborhood restaurant has an array of housemade Belgian waffle dishes, from berry-topped to a classic chicken-and-waffle combo. For something wildly different, try the red velvet waffle topped with Ghirardelli white chocolate chips, cream cheese drizzle, whipped cream and powdered sugar. 5312 Old Redwood Highway N., Petaluma, 707-658-7777

River Front Cafe

The riverside cafe’s Belgian waffle is topped with fresh strawberries, powdered sugar and whipped cream. 224 B St., Petaluma, 707-347-5147, riverfront.cafe

Cafe Mimosa

Cafe Mimosa serves waffles at all three of its locations — topped with berries, powdered sugar and mascarpone. 417 N. McDowell Blvd., Petaluma, 707-658-2795; 451 Rohnert Park Expressway, Rohnert Park, 707-595-3764; 456 College Ave., Santa Rosa, 707-293-9450, cafemimosaaa.com, instagram.com/cafe_mimosaaa

Beer Baron Bar & Kitchen

Take your bar bites to the next level with Beer Baron’s fried chicken and waffles, served with Fresno chile slaw, maple syrup and bacon butter. For dessert, try a churro waffle, topped with vanilla bean ice cream and sprinkled with cinnamon and sugar. 614 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-757-9294, beerbaronsr.com

Bésame Mucho

For a decadent brunch, try the Belgium-style waffles topped with berries, whipped cream and chocolate syrup. 115 Fourth St., Santa Rosa, 707-308-4150, besamemuchosr.com

Americana

A waffle, which can be made gluten-free, is served with housemade vanilla cider maple syrup, whipped cream and seasonal fruit. Available at both Santa Rosa and Sebastopol locations. 205 Fifth St., Suite A, Santa Rosa, 707-755-1548; 162 N. Main St., Sebastopol, 707-827-3309, americanasonomacounty.com

Fandee’s Restaurant

Fandee’s Belgian waffle is served with maple syrup and fresh berries. Make it a meal (for an extra $7) with two eggs any style and two pieces of bacon or sausage. Waffle add-ons ($2 each) include bananas and chocolate chips. 7824 Covert Lane, Sebastopol, 707-829-2642, fandeesrestaurant.com

Howard Station Cafe

The locomotive-themed cafe in Occidental includes a variety of waffle dishes on its menu, from a simple Belgian waffle to more decadent versions like the chocolate chip and cream waffle. A favorite is the peaches and cream waffle. 3611 Bohemian Hwy., Occidental, 707-874-2838, howardstationcafe.com

Saucy Mama’s Jook Joint

The cornbread waffle is the perfect accompaniment to the buttermilk fried chicken or spicy hot link. 16632 Highway 116, Guerneville, 707-604-7184, saucymamasjookjoint.com

Quail & Condor

The Healdsburg bakery and cafe features a sourdough waffle on its breakfast menu, served with cultured butter, apricot jam and Vermont maple syrup. 44 Mill St., Unit J, Healdsburg, 707-473-8254, quailandcondor.com

title: Sonoma’s New Smash Restaurant Leans Into Fast-Casual Burgers
summary:
Chef Ari Weiswasser brings fast-casual smashburgers to the Sonoma Plaza at new family-friendly Smash restaurant.

The post Sonoma’s New Smash Restaurant Leans Into Fast-Casual Burgers appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
Chef Ari Weiswasser, the restaurateur behind Glen Ellen Star and Stella, opened Smash in May, a burger-focused fast-casual restaurant on Sonoma Plaza.

After years spent crafting polished farm-to-table cuisine, Weiswasser is leaning into something simpler, faster and a lot less fussy.

Located in the former Taub Family Outpost space, Smash is bright and contemporary, with self-service ordering, bar seating, communal tables and a small patio.

There’s plenty of noise and action inside, fitting for a family-friendly restaurant built around approachable prices. Diners seeking a quieter experience may want to take their burgers to go or sit at one of the outdoor tables.

Upstairs, the Beacon speakeasy offers a more adult setting, serving craft cocktails alongside the full Smash menu.

Open 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily. 497 First St. W., Sonoma, 707-721-1107, instagram.com/smashsonoma, smashsonoma.com

title: Bonnie Bagels Brings East Coast Classic to Sebastopol
summary:
Recently opened in the former Hippizzazz pizza space — near longtime Sebastopol favorite Grateful Bagel — Bonnie Bagels is banking on the East Coast classic.

The post Bonnie Bagels Brings East Coast Classic to Sebastopol appeared first on Sonoma Magazine.
content:
A small Sebastopol cafe has finally cracked the code on East Coast bagels in Sonoma County.

Bonnie Bagels opened in mid-August with kettle-cooked bagels — boiled and baked, as they should be — and a line out the door.

Yes, there are other good bagels in Sonoma County. But until now, I wouldn’t have called them East Coast great. Bonnie’s aren’t just East Coast great. They’re New York great: crisp on the outside, chewy on the inside and, best of all, available in salt.

“It’s a secret hint to a certain kind of person that we’re the real deal. It’s classic East Coast,” said executive chef Greg Kalergis.

Owner Michael Sousa, who grew up near Boston, knew it was time to open a shop about 18 months ago, when the stars aligned. The former Hippizzazz Pizza space across from HopMonk was vacant. He had friends from Bageltopia in Berkeley willing to mentor the fledgling venture. And he had recently met Kalergis, now his executive chef, at a family Thanksgiving.

After more than a year of planning and construction — and plenty of flak for opening a bagel shop within spitting distance of longtime Sebastopol favorite Grateful Bagel — Sousa soldiered on.

“I understand the awkwardness of it,” Sousa said. “But the benefits of bringing this to the community outweighed that. I’m hopeful that we can provide something different enough that we can coexist in harmony.”

Besides salt bagels, the cafe offers the usual lineup of plain, sesame, poppy seed, onion and everything, along with more California-leaning flavors such as cheddar jalapeño and Asiago. Schmears include caper dill, smoked salmon, scallion, green olive and chile crisp.

There are also gluten-free bagels and vegan cream cheese, plus breakfast sandwiches and open-faced lox, tuna salad and egg salad bagels. Espresso drinks and coffee round things out.

On opening day, the shop sold out within three hours. The same thing happened the next day.

After two days to regroup, the team is back with more of everything — especially those brilliantly boiled-and-baked bagels.

As for the odd, half-finished sign that currently says “Bonnie Bag”? Painting was interrupted by permitting issues. The owners expect to finish it in the next couple of weeks.

Open 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. 280 S. Main St., Sebastopol, bonniebagels.com
